source_text: Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τὸ χρυσοφορεῖν καὶ τὸ ἐσθῆτι μαλακωτέρᾳ χρῆσθαι οὐ τέλεον περικοπτέον, χαλινωτέον δὲ τὰς ἀλόγους τῶν ὁρμῶν, μὴ εἰς τὸ ἁβροδίαιτον ἡμᾶς ἐνσείσωσιν φέρουσαι ὑπὸ πολλῆς τῆς ἀνέσεως ἐξαρπάσασαι· δεινὴ γὰρ ἡ τρυφὴ εἰς κόρον ἐξοκείλασα σκιρτῆσαι καὶ ἀναχαιτίσαι καὶ τὸν ἡνίοχον, [καὶ] τὸν παιδαγωγόν, ἀποσείσασθαι, ὃς πόρρωθεν ἀνακόπτων τὰς ἡνίας ἄγει καὶ φέρει πρὸς σωτηρίαν τὸν ἵππον τὸν ἀνθρώπειον, τὸ ἄλογον μέρος τῆς ψυχῆς τὸ περὶ ἡδονὰς καὶ ὀρέξεις ἐπιψόγους καὶ λίθους καὶ χρυσίον καὶ ἐσθῆτα ποικίλην καὶ τὴν ἄλλην χλιδὴν ἐκθηριούμενον· ἐκεῖνο μάλιστα ἐν νῷ ἔχοντες τὸ εἰρημένον ἁγίως »τὴν ἀναστροφὴν ὑμῶν ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἔχοντες καλήν, ἵνα ἐν ᾧ καταλαλοῦσιν ὑμῶν ὡς κακοποιῶν, ἐκ τῶν καλῶν ἔργων ἐποπτεύσαντες δοξάσωσι τὸν θεόν.« δίδωσιν οὖν ἡμῖν ὁ παιδαγωγὸς ἐσθῆτι χρῆσθαι τῇ λιτῇ, χρόᾳ δὲ τῇ λευκῇ, ὡς προειρήκαμεν, ἵνα μὴ τέχνῃ ποικιλλομένῃ, φύσει δὲ γεννωμένῃ οἰκειούμενοι, πᾶν ὅσον ἀπατηλὸν καὶ τῆς ἀληθείας καταψευδόμενον παρωσάμενοι τὸ μονότροπον καὶ μονοπρόσωπον τῆς ἀληθείας ἀσπασώμεθα. ἁβροδίαιτον ὀνειδίζων νεανίαν ὁ Σοφοκλῆς λέγει· γυναικομίμοις ἐμπρέπεις ἐσθήμασιν. ὡς γὰρ στρατιώτου καὶ ναύτου καὶ ἄρχοντος, οὕτως δὲ καὶ σώφρονός ἐστιν οἰκεία στολὴ ἡ ἀπερίεργος καὶ εὐσχήμων καὶ καθάριος. παρ᾿ ὃ καὶ ὁ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ περὶ τῆς λέπρας διὰ Μωυσέως τεθεὶς νόμος τὸ ποικίλον καὶ πολύστικτον ὡς οὐχ ὅσιον ἀπωθεῖται ταῖς ποικίλαις τοῦ ὄφεως φολίσιν ἐοικός. τὸν γοῦν μηκέτι διηνθισμένον ποικιλίᾳ χρωμάτων, ὅλον δὲ λευκωθέντα δι᾿ ὅλων ἀπὸ κεφαλῆς ἄκρας ἄχρι ποδῶν ἐσχάτων καθαρὸν εἶναι ἐθέλει, ἵνα κατὰ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ σώματος μετάβασιν τὸ ποικίλον καὶ πανοῦργον τῆς διανοίας μεθέμενοι πάθος τὸ ἀποίκιλτον καὶ ἀνενδοίαστον τῆς ἀληθείας ἁπλοῦν ἀγαπήσωμεν χρῶμα. ὁ δὲ καὶ ἐν τούτῳ ἄρα ζηλωτὴν Μωυσέως, ὁ πάντα ἄριστος Πλάτων, ὑφὴν ἐκείνην ἀποδέχεται, ᾗ μὴ πλέον ἔργον πρόσεστι γυναικὸς σώφρονος· »χρώματα δὲ λευκὰ πρέποντα ἂν εἴη σεμνότητι καὶ ἄλλοθι« λέγει »καὶ ἐν ὑφῇ· βάμματα δὲ μὴ προσφέρειν ἀλλ᾿ ἢ πρὸς τὰ πολέμου κοσμήματα.« εἰρηνικοῖς ἄρα ἀνθρώποις καὶ φωτεινοῖς κατάλληλον τὸ λευκόν. ὡς οὖν τὰ σημεῖα τὰ ἐγγυτάτω ὄντα τῶν αἰτίων παρόντα σημαίνει, μᾶλλον δὲ δείκνυσι τὴν τοῦ ἀποτελέσαντος ὕπαρξιν, οἷον καπνὸς μὲν πῦρ, εὔχροια δὲ καὶ εὐσφυξία ὑγίειαν, οὕτως καὶ παρ᾿ ἡμῖν ἡ τοιάδε στολὴ τοῦ ἤθους τὴν κατάστασιν ἐνδείκνυται. καθάριος δὲ καὶ ἀφελὴς ἡ σωφροσύνη, ἐπεὶ ἡ μὲν καθαριότης ἕξις ἐστὶν παρασκευαστικὴ διαίτης καθαρᾶς καὶ ἀμιγοῦς αἰσχροῖς, ἡ δὲ ἀφέλεια ἕξις ἀφαιρετικὴ τῶν περιττῶν. ἡ δὲ στερεὰ ἐσθὴς καὶ μάλιστα ἡ ἄγναφος ἀποστέγει τὸ θερμὸν τὸ ἐν τῷ σώματι, οὐχ ὅτι ἐν αὑτῇ ἔχει τὴν θερμότητα ἡ ἐσθής, ἀλλ᾿ ὅτι τὴν ἐν τῷ σώματι ἐξιοῦσαν ἀναστρέφει καὶ πάροδον αὐτῇ οὐ παρέχει, εἰ δὲ καὶ ἐμπέσοι τις, συλλαβοῦσα αὐτὴν ἐν αὑτῇ ἔχει καὶ ὑπ᾿ αὐτῆς θερμανθεῖσα ἀντιθερμαίνει τὸ σῶμα, δι᾿ ὃ καὶ χειμῶνος μάλιστα ταύτῃ χρηστέον· εὔκολος δὲ αὕτη· εὐκολία δέ ἐστιν ἕξις ἀπέριττος προσδεκτικὴ τῶν πρὸς τὸ ἀνελλιπὲς ἐξαρκούντων εἰς τὸν κατὰ λόγον, τὸν ὑγιῆ καὶ μακάριον, βίον.
pass_a_gloss: For this reason, therefore, we must not completely cut off wearing gold and using softer clothing, but we must restrain the irrational impulses, lest they lead us into luxury, having snatched us away under much relaxation; for luxury is terrible, having slipped into excess, and it makes us leap and dance and throw off the charioteer and the tutor, who, looking from afar, guides and leads the human horse, the irrational part of the soul, towards salvation, concerning pleasures and desires, and it makes us fond of ornaments and gold and varied clothing and other frivolity; having this in mind, what was said holy, 'having your conduct among the nations good, so that in what they speak against you as evil-doers, they may glorify God from your good works'; the tutor, therefore, gives us permission to use simple clothing and white color, as we said before, so that, not being fond of varied art, but of natural birth, we may reject everything that is deceptive and false and welcome the simple and single-faced truth; Sophocles, reproaching a young man for luxury, says, 'you are conspicuous in womanly clothing'; for just as a soldier and a sailor and a ruler have their own proper and modest and clean clothing, so also does the self-controlled person; and the law given through Moses about leprosy rejects the varied and much-spun as not holy, being similar to the varied scales of a snake; for it wants the one who is no longer dyed with varied colors, but completely whitened from head to foot, to be clean, so that, having changed from the body, we may love the simple and unchanging color of truth, having left behind the varied and cunning passion of the mind; and Plato, the best of all, who is an emulator of Moses, accepts this weaving, in which no more work is added than that of a self-controlled woman; 'white colors, therefore, are suitable for dignity and also for weaving', he says, 'and not to apply dyes except for war ornaments'; therefore, white is suitable for peaceful and bright people; just as the nearest signs indicate the presence of the causes, or rather show the existence of the one who brought them to completion, such as smoke indicates fire, and good color and good breathing indicate health, so also our clothing indicates the condition of our character; for self-control is pure and simple, since purity is a habit that prepares for a pure and unmixed diet, and simplicity is a habit that removes what is superfluous; and a thick and especially a unwashed garment keeps the body warm, not because the garment has warmth in itself, but because it turns back the warmth that is escaping from the body and does not provide a passage for it, and if some cold air enters, it holds it in itself and, having been warmed by it, warms the body in return, for which reason we must use it especially in winter; and it is easy to use; ease of use is a habit that is without superfluity, receptive of what is sufficient for a life according to reason, healthy and happy

pass_b_english: For this reason we must not utterly forbid wearing gold or using finer clothing, but we must bridle the irrational impulses of our nature lest they drag us into luxury, snatching us away in a flood of self-indulgence. Luxury is a terrible thing: once it slips into excess it makes us leap and kick, throwing off both the charioteer and the tutor who, watching from afar, pulls the reins and guides the human horse toward salvation. That horse is the irrational part of the soul, the part that lusts after shameful pleasures and desires—ornaments, gold, varied clothing, and every other frivolity. With this in mind we recall the holy command: "Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God" (1 Peter 2:12). Accordingly the Tutor permits us to wear simple clothing of a white color, as we said before, so that we may cling not to artificial variety but to what is natural, rejecting everything deceptive and false and embracing the straightforward, single-faced truth.

Sophocles rebukes a luxurious young man: "You are conspicuous in womanish garments." Just as a soldier, a sailor, and a ruler each has his own proper, modest, and clean attire, so also does the self-controlled person. The law given through Moses concerning leprosy rejects the variegated and heavily spun as unholy, because it resembles the mottled scales of a serpent. That law requires the sufferer to be no longer dyed with varied colors but completely whitened from head to foot, so that—passing from the body as a figure—we may put off the varied, cunning passion of the mind and love the simple, unchanging color of truth. Plato, the best of all men and an emulator of Moses, accepts that plain weave which demands no more work than a modest woman would give. "White colors," he says, "are fitting for dignity, both elsewhere and in cloth; dyes should be used only for the trappings of war." White is therefore suited to people who are peaceful and bright.

Just as the nearest signs indicate the presence of their causes—or better, reveal the existence of the one who produced them, as smoke shows fire and healthy color and breathing show health—so our clothing displays the state of our character. Self-control is pure and simple: purity is a habit that prepares a clean, unmixed way of life, and simplicity is a habit that strips away the superfluous. A thick garment, especially an unwashed one, retains the body's warmth—not because the cloth possesses heat of its own, but because it turns back the warmth escaping from the body and gives it no exit. If cold air penetrates, the fabric traps it, warms it, and returns the heat to the body. For this reason such clothing is especially useful in winter, and it is easy to use. Ease of use is a habit free of excess, receptive of what suffices for a life lived according to reason—a healthy and blessed life.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass A provides a literal rendering, while Pass B provides a fluent, readable version that maintains the theological and philosophical distinctions. The scripture citation (1 Peter 2:12) added in Pass B is a correct identification of the quoted/alluded text 'τὴν ἀναστροφὴν ὑμῶν ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἔχοντες καλήν'.
